question: Directive (EU) 2015/849 requires that credit institutions implement enhanced measures regarding politically exposed persons (PEPs), their family members and close associates, including the identification of the source of their assets and funds. Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 confirms this framework, including for occasional transactions.

According to public information based on Spanish legal proceedings, an investigation is under way into the possible illicit origin of funds linked to former Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero and his inner circle, including the early repayment of a mortgage of nearly EUR 500 000 from a joint account with his wife.

Without assuming criminal liability, the case raises an issue: if an ordinary EU citizen is subject to strict banking controls for minor transactions, a person holding public office in the EU must be subject to enhanced, documented and verifiable controls. 1.

Does the Commission consider that the current framework ensures that credit institutions document the origin of funds used for significant mortgage repayments made by persons holding public office or by those linked to them?
Is the Commission, together with the European Banking Authority and national financial intelligence units, assessing whether suspicious transaction reports function properly for domestic PEPs?
What role does the Commission assign to the future Anti-Money Laundering Authority in the supervision of higher-risk credit institutions in similar cases?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) The EU anti-money laundering framework1 requires obliged entities, including credit institutions, to apply enhanced customer due diligence measures in respect of politically exposed persons, their family members and persons known to be close associates.

These measures include taking reasonable measures to establish the source of wealth and the source of funds involved in business relationships or transactions. Compliance with these requirements is the responsibility of obliged entities and is checked by supervisors. Ensuring the proper reporting of suspicious transactions by obliged entities is the task of financial intelligence units and supervisors.

The Commission continues to monitor the effective implementation of the EU anti-money laundering framework. Under the new EU anti-money laundering package, the Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA)2 will contribute to ensuring consistent and effective supervision across the EU.

AMLA will directly supervise selected high-risk cross-border financial sector entities and will coordinate and support the supervisory system as a whole. AMLA will also support cooperation and information exchange among supervisors and financial intelligence units, thereby strengthening the consistent application of EU anti-money laundering rules.
